title: What are non-deterministic functions in Spark (`rand`, `uuid`, `monotonically_increasing_id`, `collect_list`, `shuffle`, `input_file_name`, `spark_partition_id`) — they return different results on multiple invocations — and why does the optimizer treat them differently (may skip predicate pushdown, may re-execute unexpectedly)?
topicTitle: What are non-deterministic functions in Spark (`rand`, `uuid`, `monotonically_in

s1_definition.profdef: Non-deterministic functions in Spark are functions that can return different results across invocations even for the same input, because they depend on randomness, state, partitioning, or ordering rather than purely on their arguments. Examples include `rand`, `randn`, `uuid`, `monotonically_increasing_id`, `shuffle`, `input_file_name`, `spark_partition_id`, and order-sensitive aggregates like `collect_list`. The Catalyst optimizer marks them non-deterministic and treats them specially: it will not push them below filters, will not reorder or duplicate them freely, and must be careful because re-executing a stage can produce different values.
s1_definition.analogy: Most functions at the National Bank are like a fixed interest formula: same inputs, same answer every time. Non-deterministic functions are like drawing a random queue token or stamping the current counter number — run it twice and you get different tokens. The planner cannot shuffle these operations around the way it safely rearranges the fixed formula, because moving or repeating them would change which token each customer got.
s1_definition.oneliner: Non-deterministic functions (rand, uuid, monotonically_increasing_id, shuffle, input_file_name, spark_partition_id, order-sensitive collect_list) return different results across runs, so Catalyst will not push them past filters or freely reorder and re-execute them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Non-deterministic functions in Spark are functions that can return different results across invocations even for the same input, because they depend on randomness, state, partitioning, or ordering rather than purely on their arguments. Examples include `rand`, `randn`, `uuid`, `monotonically_increasing_id`, `shuffle`, `input_file_name`, `spark_partition_id`, and order-sensitive aggregates like `collect_list`. The Catalyst optimizer marks them non-deterministic and treats them specially: it will not push them below filters, will not reorder or duplicate them freely, and must be careful because re-executing a stage can produce different values.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Most functions at the National Bank are like a fixed interest formula: same inputs, same answer every time. Non-deterministic functions are like drawing a random queue token or stamping the current counter number — run it twice and you get different tokens. The planner cannot shuffle these operations around the way it safely rearranges the fixed formula, because moving or repeating them would change which token each customer got.

**One line to remember:** Non-deterministic functions (rand, uuid, monotonically_increasing_id, shuffle, input_file_name, spark_partition_id, order-sensitive collect_list) return different results across runs, so Catalyst will not push them past filters or freely reorder and re-execute them.

sections.s2_technical:
A deterministic function returns the same output for the same input every time, which lets Catalyst move, combine, duplicate, and reorder it safely. A non-deterministic function breaks that assumption. `rand` and `randn` draw from a random number generator. `uuid` generates a fresh identifier each call. `monotonically_increasing_id` produces increasing ids whose exact values depend on the partition layout, so they are not stable across runs. `shuffle` randomly reorders an array. `input_file_name` and `spark_partition_id` depend on where the data physically lives and how it is partitioned. `collect_list` is non-deterministic in the sense that the order of collected elements depends on execution and partitioning unless you impose an order.

Catalyst explicitly tracks a `deterministic` flag on expressions, and non-deterministic ones get special handling. The optimizer will not push a non-deterministic expression below a filter or through operators in ways that could change its evaluation count, because if it did, a value computed before versus after a filter could differ. It avoids common-subexpression elimination that would collapse two separate random draws into one. And it cannot assume a re-run yields the same values, which matters because Spark can recompute a lost partition after a failure or recompute an uncached DataFrame referenced twice; in both cases a non-deterministic column can produce different values on the recomputation.

The practical consequences are concrete. Predicate pushdown may be skipped around these functions, which can read more data than you expect. A column of `monotonically_increasing_id` is not a stable key and should not be relied on as a reproducible identifier across runs or joins. If you reference a DataFrame with a `rand` column twice without caching, the two references can see different random values. The fix for stability is to materialize — cache or write out the DataFrame — so the non-deterministic values are computed once and frozen, or to seed `rand(seed)` for repeatability within a run.

A senior nuance: when you need a stable unique id, prefer a seeded approach, a hash of stable columns, or write-then-read so the ids are fixed; and when you use `collect_list` and order matters, impose it with `sort_array` or a windowed ordering, since Spark does not guarantee element order otherwise.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank assigned surrogate ids to transactions with `monotonically_increasing_id` and reused the DataFrame in two places without caching, so the two uses disagreed on ids and a join produced wrong matches. This is exactly the non-determinism-on-recompute problem.

Problem 2 — A sampling job used `rand` to pick audit samples but referenced the sampled DataFrame twice, getting different samples each time. Caching fixes this by freezing the random values.

Problem 3 — A lineage column needed the source file name via `input_file_name`, which is non-deterministic in that it depends on physical layout. This illustrates a legitimate but non-deterministic function.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`NonDeterministicDemo`) that shows `monotonically_increasing_id` and `rand` changing across references, then stabilizes them by caching, for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/nondeterministic_demo.py
# Shows non-deterministic functions and how to stabilize them for the bank.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from ids.id_strategies import IdStrategies

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("NonDeterministicDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return SparkSession.builder.appName("NonDeterministicDemo").getOrCreate()

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    df = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", 50000.0), ("CUR3001", 25000.0), ("SAV2001", 12000.0)],
        ["account_id", "amount"])
    strat = IdStrategies()

    # UNSTABLE: monotonically_increasing_id + rand recomputed on each reference
    unstable = strat.unstable_ids(df)
    log.warning("Unstable ids/rand can DIFFER across references (not cached):")
    unstable.show()

    # STABILIZED: cache so non-deterministic values are computed ONCE and frozen
    stable = strat.stabilized_ids(df)
    log.info("Stabilized (cached) ids/rand - frozen across references:")
    stable.show(); stable.show()   # both show the SAME frozen values

    # Deterministic alternative: a stable hash-based surrogate key
    log.info("Deterministic hash key (reproducible across runs):")
    strat.hash_key(df).show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/ids/id_strategies.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class IdStrategies:
    """Contrasts non-deterministic ids with stabilized/deterministic ones."""

    def unstable_ids(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # monotonically_increasing_id + rand are non-deterministic
        return df.withColumn("mono_id", F.monotonically_increasing_id()) \
                 .withColumn("rnd", F.rand())

    def stabilized_ids(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # cache() freezes the non-deterministic values after first materialization
        out = df.withColumn("mono_id", F.monotonically_increasing_id()) \
                .withColumn("rnd", F.rand(seed=42)).cache()
        out.count()   # materialize to freeze
        return out

    def hash_key(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # DETERMINISTIC: same inputs -> same key, reproducible across runs
        return df.withColumn("sk",
                             F.sha2(F.concat_ws("|", "account_id", "amount"), 256))
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three rows for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: `unstable_ids` adds `monotonically_increasing_id` and `rand`. These are marked non-deterministic by Catalyst. If this DataFrame is referenced more than once without caching, Spark may recompute it, and each recomputation can yield different ids and random values.

Step 2: Because the optimizer treats these as non-deterministic, it will not push a later filter below them and will not collapse two random draws into one, so the plan is more constrained than with deterministic columns.

Step 3: `stabilized_ids` adds the same columns but calls `cache` and then `count` to materialize. This computes the non-deterministic values once and stores the result as blocks, so every subsequent reference sees the exact same frozen ids and random numbers. Showing it twice yields identical output.

Step 4: `hash_key` builds a deterministic surrogate key with sha2 over stable columns. The same inputs always produce the same key, so it is reproducible across runs and safe to use as a join key, unlike `monotonically_increasing_id`.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  df + monotonically_increasing_id()/rand()   ← NON-DETERMINISTIC
        │
        ├─ referenced twice, NOT cached ─▶ recompute ─▶ DIFFERENT values ✗
        │        (optimizer: no pushdown past these, no CSE, re-exec risk)
        │
        └─ cache()+count() ─▶ values computed ONCE ─▶ FROZEN across refs ✓

  Deterministic alternative:
  df + sha2(stable cols) ─▶ same inputs → same key → reproducible ✓
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Non-deterministic functions in Spark are functions that can return different results across invocations even for the same input, because they depend on randomness, state, physical partitioning, or ordering rather than purely on their arguments. The ones I name are rand and randn for randomness, uuid for fresh identifiers, monotonically_increasing_id whose values depend on partition layout, shuffle which randomly reorders an array, input_file_name and spark_partition_id which depend on where data physically lives, and order-sensitive aggregates like collect_list whose element order is not guaranteed. Catalyst explicitly tracks a deterministic flag on every expression, and these get marked non-deterministic.

The optimizer treats them specially for correctness. It will not push a non-deterministic expression below a filter, because a value computed before versus after a filter could differ, so predicate pushdown may be skipped and you can end up reading more data than expected. It avoids common-subexpression elimination that would collapse two independent random draws into one. And it cannot assume a re-run produces the same values, which matters because Spark recomputes lost partitions after a failure and recomputes an uncached DataFrame that is referenced twice. In both cases a non-deterministic column can yield different values on the recomputation.

At the National Bank of India this caused a real bug: we generated surrogate ids with monotonically_increasing_id, reused the DataFrame in two places without caching, and the two uses disagreed on ids so a join matched the wrong rows. The fix was to materialize the DataFrame by caching it so the ids were computed once and frozen, and for a truly reproducible key we switched to a deterministic sha2 hash of stable columns. The guidance I give is that monotonically_increasing_id is not a stable key, that you should cache or write-then-read to freeze non-deterministic values, that you can seed rand for repeatability within a run, and that when collect_list order matters you must impose it explicitly because Spark does not guarantee it.
